topic.title: Addition polymerisation
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Part of the organic chemistry question on the C2 paper at both tiers. Foundation: the process named [2] and the polymer named from its monomer [1]. Higher: a structural equation or repeat unit [2], or the monomer deduced from a section of chain [2], often with an unfamiliar monomer.
mustMemorise: A monomer is a small molecule that can join to others to form a polymer
A polymer is a very long chain molecule made from many monomers
The process is addition polymerisation: both words are marks
Only a monomer with a C=C can form an addition polymer
Repeat unit: single C–C bond, a bond through each bracket, n after the bracket
n goes in front of the monomer and after the bracket
The repeat unit has exactly the monomer's atoms
onFormulaSheet: Relative atomic masses and the Periodic Table (Chemistry Data Leaflet)
notOnThisSpec: Natural polymers such as proteins, starch and DNA
The free-radical mechanism of addition polymerisation

externalRefs.credit: Cognito, GCSE Chemistry: addition polymers and polymerisation

given: Relative atomic masses and the Periodic Table (Chemistry Data Leaflet)
mustKnow: Monomer and polymer, and the name addition polymerisation
Poly(ethene) from ethene and poly(chloroethene) from chloroethene
The four features of a drawn repeat unit
n on both sides of the structural equation

mustBeAbleTo: Describe how monomers join to form a very long chain molecule, a polymer, and name the process addition polymerisation
Name poly(ethene) and poly(chloroethene) from their monomers, and a monomer from its polymer's name
Explain why a monomer for addition polymerisation needs a C=C
Draw the repeat unit with a single C–C bond, a bond through each bracket and n (Higher)
Write the structural equation for the polymerisation of ethene and of chloroethene, with n on both sides (Higher)
Deduce the repeat unit from any simple alkene monomer, and the monomer from a section of chain (Higher)
Check a repeat unit by its atoms and by four bonds at every carbon
sheet.howExamined: Inside the organic chemistry question of the C2 paper (1 hour 15 minutes; 70 marks at Foundation, 80 at Higher; calculator and Data Leaflet). Foundation asks for names: the process [2], one mark for each word, and the polymer made from ethene [1]. Higher adds the drawing: a structural equation or repeat unit [2], one mark for the structure and one for the brackets and n, or the monomer from a section of chain [2], often with a monomer you have not met. Outcomes 2.5.18 and 2.5.19 are Higher only.
traps: The polymer made from ethene left unnamed or named wrongly: write poly, then the monomer in brackets (Summer 2025 C2 F Q4)
Polymerisation given as the process without the word addition, which loses one of the two marks
The C=C kept inside the repeat unit, which gives each carbon five bonds
Bonds stopping short of the brackets, so the drawing no longer shows a chain
n missing in front of the monomer or after the bracket
A monomer worked back from a chain but written without its C=C, so it comes out as an alkane
A carbon drawn with three or five bonds: the polymer equation went fairly well, but a displayed formula in the same organic question was drawn poorly (Summer 2023 C2 H Q4)
A trade name such as PVC written where the chemical name is asked for

steps.working: The monomers add on to one another to make a very long chain, and nothing else is formed: addition polymerisation.
steps.decision: Both words carry a mark. Polymerisation on its own loses the first one.

steps.working: Poly, then the monomer's name in brackets: poly(chloroethene).
steps.decision: Build the name from the monomer every time. PVC is its everyday name; when a question says name, it wants the chemical one.

options: Because the polymer is many chloroethene units joined together
Because the polymer still contains a C=C
Because chlorine is the most reactive atom in it
whyMenu.explain: The name says what the chain is made of: many chloroethene units. The C=C is exactly what the polymer no longer has.

steps.working: Draw chloroethene with its C=C and n in front, an arrow, then the two carbons again joined by a single bond, with the Cl and the three H exactly where they were.
steps.decision: One of the two bonds in the C=C is what opens. If the double bond were still there, each carbon would end up with five bonds.

steps.working: Add a bond out of each carbon through a square bracket, and write n after the closing bracket.
steps.decision: The bonds through the brackets show the chain carrying on; n on both sides says n monomers make one chain of n units. That is the second drawing mark.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) Addition polymerisation. (b) Poly(chloroethene). (c) n CH2=CHCl → a repeat unit of two carbons joined by a single bond, carrying Cl and three H, in square brackets with a bond through each bracket and n after the closing bracket.

steps.working: Along the chain the same two-carbon pattern repeats: one carbon with two hydrogens, the next with one hydrogen and a CH3 group.
steps.decision: A repeat unit always has two carbons in the main chain, because each monomer's C=C brought two. A one-carbon or three-carbon unit cannot be right.

options: Because each monomer's double bond joined two carbons, and both of them end up in the chain
Because polymers always have an even number of hydrogen atoms
Because the chain breaks into pairs when it is heated
whyMenu.explain: The two carbons of each C=C become two neighbouring carbons in the chain, so the pattern repeats every two carbons.

steps.working: Take one two-carbon unit and remove the two bonds that joined it to its neighbours.
steps.decision: Those bonds were made when the monomers joined, so they are the ones that go.

steps.working: Join the two carbons with a double bond, keeping the groups: H and H on one carbon, H and CH3 on the other.
steps.decision: Putting the C=C back is the step most often missed. Without it the molecule is an alkane, and an alkane cannot polymerise.

steps.working: Three carbons and a double bond: propene, C3H6.
steps.decision: Count the CH3 carbon too. It hangs off the main chain but it belongs to the monomer.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) CH2=CH–CH3: two carbons joined by a double bond, with two H on one and one H and a CH3 on the other. (b) Propene.

workedExamples.stem:
One chain of poly(chloroethene) has a relative formula mass of 50 000.
(a) Calculate the relative formula mass of its repeat unit. [2]
(b) Calculate how many chloroethene molecules joined to make the chain. [1]
Use relative atomic masses from the Data Leaflet.

steps.working: The repeat unit has the same atoms as the monomer, chloroethene: C2H3Cl.
steps.decision: Nothing is lost when the monomers join, so the repeat unit's formula is the monomer's. You do not need to draw anything to know it.

options: Because addition polymerisation forms no other product, so every atom of the monomer stays
Because the double bond has no mass
Because the chlorine is lost when the chain forms
whyMenu.explain: No second product, so no atom leaves: the repeat unit is one monomer's worth of atoms, rearranged only in its bonding.

steps.decision: Chlorine is 35.5 on the leaflet, and there is one chlorine atom, not a Cl2 molecule.
Each monomer became exactly one repeat unit, so the number of units is the number of monomers.

twin.stem: One chain of poly(propene) has a relative formula mass of 21 000. Propene is C₃H₆. How many propene molecules joined to make the chain? Use relative atomic masses from the Data Leaflet.

items.stem: What is the functional group of the alkenes?
items.skill: Prerequisite from c2-alkenes; you are not expected to have met polymers yet

options.feedback: The C=C. This lesson is about what happens when thousands of those double bonds open at once.
That is the alcohols' group. The alkenes' is the carbon-to-carbon double bond.
Every hydrocarbon has C–H bonds, so they cannot be what makes the alkenes different. The C=C is.

items.stem: How many covalent bonds does a carbon atom form in a stable molecule?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 covalent bonding and c2-homologous-series-alkanes

options.feedback: Four. Counting to four at every carbon is the check you will use on every repeat unit you draw.
Oxygen forms two. Carbon forms four, and a drawing where it has three or five is wrong.
It never changes, which is what makes it such a useful check on a drawing.

items.stem: Ethene reacts with bromine in an addition reaction. What happens to its double bond?

options.text: one of the two bonds opens, and an atom joins each carbon
options.feedback: That is addition. Polymerisation is the same move, except that the thing joining each carbon is the next ethene molecule.

options.text: both bonds break, and the molecule splits in two
options.feedback: The carbons stay joined, by a single bond. Only one of the two bonds opens.

options.text: a hydrogen atom is swapped for a bromine atom
options.feedback: That would be substitution, which leaves a second product. Addition makes one product and nothing else.

options.text: a very long chain molecule made when many monomers join together
options.feedback: Long chain, many monomers. Those are the two ideas a definition needs.

options.text: a small molecule with a double bond that can join to others
options.feedback: That is the monomer. The polymer is what thousands of them make.
A polymer is one kind of molecule, and it contains no C=C at all once it has formed.

options.text: a molecule with many double bonds
options.feedback: The double bonds are what opened to make the chain. A polymer made this way has only single bonds along it.

items.stem: Give the full name of the process that turns ethene into poly(ethene).

options.feedback: Both words, and both are marks.
Half the name, so half the marks. The scheme also wants the word addition.
Cracking breaks big molecules into smaller ones; this process joins small ones into a big one.
Fermentation makes ethanol from sugar. Joining monomers into a chain is addition polymerisation.

items.stem: Name the polymer made from ethene.
items.skill: Name a polymer from its monomer

options.feedback: Poly, then the monomer's name in brackets.
The chain has only single bonds, but the name still comes from the monomer, and the monomer is ethene.
Ethanol is an alcohol, not an alkene. The monomer here is ethene.
There is no chlorine in ethene. That name mixes up the two polymers CCEA names.

items.stem: Which of these molecules could be a monomer for an addition polymer?
items.skill: Recognise a monomer by its C=C

options.feedback: It has a C=C, so it can polymerise: its polymer is poly(propene).
An alkane: only single bonds, all in use, so nothing can open.
An alcohol with no C=C. Addition polymerisation needs a double bond to open.
One carbon and four single bonds: no double bond, so no way to join into a chain.

items.stem: In a drawn repeat unit, what passes through each bracket?
items.skill: The features of a repeat unit

options.text: a bond, showing that the chain carries on
options.feedback: A bond through each bracket. Stopping it inside the bracket loses the mark.
The hydrogens stay on their carbons inside the brackets. What crosses the bracket is a bond.
n goes after the closing bracket, low down, not through it.
The double bond is gone once the chain forms. It is a single bond that crosses each bracket.

items.stem: Which atoms does one repeat unit of poly(chloroethene) contain?

options.text: 2 C, 3 H and 1 Cl, the same as chloroethene
options.feedback: The same atoms as the monomer, because nothing leaves when the monomers join.
That keeps all four of ethene's hydrogens and adds the chlorine too. The chlorine took one hydrogen's place.

options.text: 2 C, 2 H and 1 Cl, because a hydrogen leaves as the bond opens
options.feedback: Nothing leaves in addition polymerisation. Only a bond changes; every atom stays.
Chloroethene has one chlorine atom. The chlorine is not there as Cl₂.

items.stem: A polymer chain repeats the pattern –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–. Which monomer was it made from?
items.skill: Work back from a polymer to its monomer

options.feedback: Put the C=C back into one two-carbon unit and count all three carbons.
The double bond has to go back in. Propane has none, so it could not have made this chain.
Ethene would give CH₂ on both carbons. The CH₃ carbon counts too, making three.
Count again: two carbons in the chain plus the one in CH₃ make three, not four.

One of the two bonds in each C=C opens, and the spare bond on each carbon links it to the next monomer, so the chain has only single bonds. findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The first two steps are right, but the double bond was never put back. With only a single bond between them, each carbon would be a bond short. Restoring the C=C gives CH₂=CHCl, which is chloroethene, the monomer CCEA names.
findTheMistake.feedback: The unit was marked off correctly. The last step of working backwards is always the same: put the C=C back. A monomer for addition polymerisation must have one, so its name ends in -ene.

prompts.prompt: What is a monomer, and what is a polymer?
prompts.answer: A monomer is a small molecule that can join to others; a polymer is the very long chain molecule made when many monomers join.

prompts.prompt: Give the full name of the process that turns ethene into poly(ethene).
prompts.answer: Addition polymerisation. Each of the two words carries a mark.

prompts.prompt: How do you name the polymer made from a monomer? Give the two examples CCEA names.
prompts.answer: Write poly, then the monomer's name in brackets: ethene gives poly(ethene) and chloroethene gives poly(chloroethene).

prompts.prompt: What is PVC called in a CCEA answer, and what is its monomer?
prompts.answer: Poly(chloroethene), made from chloroethene, whose older name is vinyl chloride.

prompts.prompt: A drawn repeat unit must show four things. What are they?
prompts.answer: Square brackets; a bond passing through each bracket; a single bond between the two carbons; and n after the closing bracket.

prompts.prompt: Why can alkenes form addition polymers when alkanes cannot?
prompts.answer: Alkenes have a C=C, and one of its two bonds can open to link to other monomers; alkanes have only single bonds, all in use.

prompts.prompt: How can you check a repeat unit you have drawn?
prompts.answer: It must contain exactly the same atoms as the monomer, and every carbon must show four bonds.

prompts.prompt: How do you find the monomer from a section of polymer chain?
prompts.answer: Mark off two neighbouring carbons that repeat, remove the bonds to the neighbours, and put the C=C back between the two carbons.

prompts.prompt: Where does n appear in the equation for the polymerisation of ethene?
prompts.answer: Twice: in front of the monomer and after the closing bracket of the repeat unit.

prompts.prompt: Give one use of poly(ethene) and one use of poly(chloroethene).
prompts.answer: Poly(ethene): carrier bags, bottles or cling film. Poly(chloroethene): window frames, drainpipes or the insulation on electric cables.

findings.asked: Give the name of the polymer that ethene makes by addition polymerisation.
findings.wentWrong: Most candidates could not name it, and many left the line blank, which the examiners read as unfamiliarity with the idea itself.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Wrote poly(ethene); the scheme also accepted polythene.
findings.rule: Poly, then the monomer's name in brackets.

findings.asked: Complete a structural equation for making poly(chloroethene), in an organic question that also asked for a drawn structure of propene.
findings.wentWrong: The polymer equation went fairly well; the displayed formula of propene in the same question was drawn poorly.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Drew the repeat unit with a single C–C bond, a bond through each bracket, and n both before the monomer and after the bracket.
findings.rule: Count four bonds at every carbon, in a repeat unit as in any structure.

insight.ruleToRemember: Monomers with a C=C join into a very long chain by addition polymerisation. Name the polymer as poly(monomer). Draw the repeat unit with a single C–C bond, a bond through each bracket and n, and check it has exactly the monomer's atoms and four bonds at every carbon.
insight.aStarSignal: Deducing the repeat unit from an unfamiliar alkene monomer, and the monomer from a section of chain, and writing the structural equation with n on both sides.
